newsitem.title: KENYA: Envoys, opposition protest at Kenya student killing.
newsitem.headline: Envoys, opposition protest at Kenya student killing.

text.p: Western embassies, human rights activists and Kenya's opposition hit out on Tuesday at a student leader's killing but police said they were not treating it as a murder.
"We deplore the violent and so far unexplained death of Solomon Muruli. We are concerned this death occurred after he received threats against his person," said a U.S. embassy official.
"We urge the authorities to give high priority to the investigation of circumstances surrounding his death. We await a full and prompt disclosure of the results," he added.
The charred body of the 23-year-old student was found on Sunday in his room at a Nairobi University hostel. Witnesses and a security officer said they heard an explosion shortly before.

One day after authorities closed down Nairobi and Egerton universities because of violent protests at Muruli's death, a police spokesman said initial evidence only suggested a fire in his room and said police were not treating his death as murder.
Police Superintendent Peter Kimanthi said there was no evidence that Muruli was killed by an explosion in his room, arguing the body was "charred but not mutilated."
"We are treating this as an unnatural death. It could be an accident, it could be one taking their own life, not murder."

Police were setting up an investigation into the death based in Nyeri, central province, to be headed by Assistant Commissioner Zebedeo Ong'uti and comprising officials of various government departments.
Relatives could appoint their own pathologist to work with a police doctor during the post mortem, Kimanthi said. He declined to answer questions from reporters.
Kimanthi said police were also investigating allegations Muruli received death threats in the week before his death and his reported abduction and torture for a week in November last year.
Muruli said he was kidnapped by police in November after complaining about conditions at the university, beaten and dumped in a churchyard. Police have denied the allegations.

"We've been following the Muruli case very carefully. We are deeply shocked by his violent death and we expect that his death will be the subject of a speedy and thorough investigation," a senior official at the British High Commission told Reuters.
"Those responsible, whatever their position, must be brought to justice." Britain is Kenya's largest foreign investor and trading partner and the two countries have close political and military ties.

The Netherlands, current holder of the European Union presidency, said through its embassy in Nairobi it was worried about recent violence against Kenyan students and it feared the death of Muruli might generate further violence.
"We have time and time again appealed to the police force to bring an end to these senseless killings of innocent and helpless Kenyans," the Kenya Human Rights Commission said.
It said the withdrawal after two days of two guards provided for Muruli after he said he was threatened "shows complicity on the part of the government, the university and the police".
It said a police inspector reportedly identified by Muruli as one of his torturers should be arrested and suspended.

Leading opposition members Raila Odinga and Paul Muite and the Law Society of Kenya condemned the death. The opposition FORD-Kenya party urged the Commonwealth to investigate the role of the Kenyan security forces in violating human rights.
Kenyan students have no political agenda, at least in public, and usually protest only about fees and conditions.
